questions.q: What is an 'article' in transactional replication terminology, per this lesson?
options: A published object, typically a table or a filtered subset of one, grouped into a publication
A single row of replicated data
The name for the distribution database
A scheduled SQL Agent job that runs replication
questions.explain: An article is the published object — usually a table, sometimes filtered — and a publication groups one or more articles.

questions.q: What does the Log Reader Agent do, and where does it run?
options: It runs on the distributor and reads the publisher's transaction log continuously for committed changes to published articles
It runs on the subscriber and applies changes directly to subscriber tables
It only runs once during initial synchronization and never again
It compresses the distribution database nightly
questions.explain: The Log Reader Agent runs on the distributor, connects to the publisher, and continuously reads the transaction log — this continuous reading is what makes replication near-real-time.

questions.q: What does the Distribution Agent do?
options: Reads queued commands from the distribution database and applies them to each subscriber in original commit order
Reads the publisher's transaction log directly
Generates the initial snapshot for synchronization
Manages backup and restore operations for the distributor
questions.explain: The Distribution Agent delivers the queued command stream to subscribers, preserving the original commit order.

questions.q: What's the difference between a push subscription and a pull subscription, per this lesson?
options: Where the Distribution Agent runs — at the distributor (push) or at the subscriber (pull)
Push subscriptions use merge replication; pull subscriptions use transactional replication
Pull subscriptions don't require a distributor at all
Push subscriptions are one-time only; pull subscriptions are continuous
questions.explain: Push vs. pull is a topology choice about where the Distribution Agent runs, not a difference in what gets delivered.

questions.q: Why does splitting change-capture (Log Reader Agent) from change-delivery (Distribution Agent) matter, per this lesson?
options: A slow or unreachable subscriber doesn't block change capture on the publisher, and the publisher's log can still be truncated once the Log Reader Agent has consumed the transactions
It has no practical benefit — it's purely a historical design accident
It allows the publisher to skip transaction logging entirely
It guarantees zero replication latency at all times
questions.explain: The split isolates the publisher's log truncation and performance from subscriber-side delivery problems, though it's also where partial failures tend to show up.
